'''Heritage tourism''' is a specific type of [[tourism]] that focus on the exploration and appreciation of a region's cultural, historical, and environmental heritage.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Jin |first1=Yang |last2=Hou |first2=Bing |last3=Kong |first3=Xiang |date=June 2024 |title=The Practice Characteristics of Authorized Heritage Discourse in Tourism: Thematic and Spatial |journal=Land |language=en |volume=13 |issue=6 |pages=816 |doi=10.3390/land13060816 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2024Land...13..816J |issn=2073-445X}}</ref> This form of tourism includes both [[Tangibility|tangible]] elements, such as [[:Category:Historic sites|historically significant sites]], [[monument]]s, and [[Artifact (archaeology)|artifacts]], and [[Intangible cultural heritage|intangible]] aspects, including [[tradition]]s, [[Customary law|customs]], and [[Ritual|practices]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Cultural Heritage {{!}} Kentucky Tourism – State of Kentucky – Visit Kentucky, Official Site |url=https://www.kentuckytourism.com/industry/tourism-resources/cultural-heritage |access-date=2023-12-13 |website=Kentucky Tourism |language=en}}</ref>

A specific subset of heritage tourism, [[Cultural tourism|cultural heritage tourism]], emphasises on the human dimension of these sites, focusing on the traditions, practices, and values that are deeply connected to them.<ref>Rosenfeld, Raymond (2008). [https://www.researchgate.net/publication/237461371_CULTURAL_AND_HERITAGE_TOURISM "Cultural and Heritage Tourism"]. Eastern Michigan University.</ref> Likewise, heritage tourism focuses specifically on the history of a region, as well as its [[natural heritage]].

Heritage tourism can look like visiting [[Historic site|historically significant locations]], engaging with local traditions ([[Folklore]]), and gaining insights into the historical and contemporary aspects of a community, culture or religion.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Zhang |first1=Juan |last2=Xiong |first2=Kangning |last3=Liu |first3=Zhaojun |last4=He |first4=Lixiang |date=2022-03-23 |title=Research progress and knowledge system of world heritage tourism: a bibliometric analysis |journal=Heritage Science |volume=10 |issue=1 |pages=42 |doi=10.1186/s40494-022-00654-0 |doi-access=free |issn=2050-7445}}</ref>

Consequently, heritage tourism also underscores the importance of preserving cultural and historical resources. This can be extremely beneficial for a region, not only by helping in the preservation of vital customs and culture, but also by contributing to the [[economic development]] and [[sustainability]] of the area.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Timothy |first=Dallen J. |date=2018-01-01 |title=Making sense of heritage tourism: Research trends in a maturing field of study |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2211973617301320 |journal=Tourism Management Perspectives |volume=25 |pages=177–180 |doi=10.1016/j.tmp.2017.11.018 |hdl=11059/14282 |issn=2211-9736|hdl-access=free }}</ref>

== History ==

In some [[Christianity|Christian]] and [[Islam]]ic traditions, the purpose of a [[pilgrimage]] was often to honor the [[shrine]] of a [[prophet]] or [[saint]], such as that of [[Muhammad]] in [[Mecca]] during the [[Islamic pilgrimage]]s of the [[Hajj]] and [[Umrah]]. Other popular pilgrimage sites in [[Europe]] included [[Lourdes]] in [[France]] and [[Canterbury]] in [[England]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Collins-Kreiner |first=Noga |date=2018-05-04 |title=Pilgrimage-Tourism: Common Themes in Different Religions |url=https://arrow.tudublin.ie/ijrtp/vol6/iss1/3 |journal=International Journal of Religious Tourism and Pilgrimage |volume=6 |issue=1 |doi=10.21427/D73428 |s2cid=150040112 |issn=2009-7379}}</ref> In some cases [[pilgrim]]s contribute significantly to the [[Economy|economies]] of certain regions.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Collins-Kreiner |first=N. |date=2010-01-01 |title=The geography of pilgrimage and tourism: Transformations and implications for applied geography |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0143622809000150 |journal=Applied Geography |volume=30 |issue=1 |pages=153–164 |doi=10.1016/j.apgeog.2009.02.001 |bibcode=2010AppGe..30..153C |issn=0143-6228|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Wu |first1=Hung-Che |last2=Chang |first2=Ya-Yuan |last3=Wu |first3=Tsung-Pao |date=2019-03-01 |title=Pilgrimage: What drives pilgrim experiential supportive intentions? |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1447677018302390 |journal=Journal of Hospitality and Tourism Management |volume=38 |pages=66–81 |doi=10.1016/j.jhtm.2018.11.001 |s2cid=261175823 |issn=1447-6770|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

For example, the rediscovery of [[Ancient Rome|ancient Roman]] ruins at [[Pompeii]] and [[Herculaneum]] stimulated an interest in the [[civilization]]s of the [[ancient world]] and travel.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Bowersock |first=G. W. |date=1978 |title=The Rediscovery of Herculaneum and Pompeii |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/41210458 |journal=The American Scholar |volume=47 |issue=4 |pages=461–470 |jstor=41210458 |issn=0003-0937}}</ref> Additionally, in the [[19th century]], there was an increase in tourism and in [[Grand Tour|grand tours of Europe]] to historical sites.<ref>{{Cite web |title=What was the Grand Tour? {{!}} Royal Museums Greenwich |url=https://www.rmg.co.uk/stories/topics/what-was-grand-tour |access-date=2023-12-13 |website=www.rmg.co.uk |language=en}}</ref> The concept of a [[Monument|historical monument]] emerged in the [[Western world]], accompanied by [[tourism]].<ref>{{Cite book |title=A Research Agenda for Heritage Tourism |publisher=Edward Elgar Publishing |year=2020 |isbn=9781789903522 |editor1=Maria Gravari-Barbas |pages=1}}</ref>

=== UNESCO World Heritage Convention ===
Heritage tourism is promoted by the [[World Heritage Convention]], which is a part of [[UNESCO]]. This stemmed from various safeguarding campaigns. The decision to build the [[Aswan Dam|Aswan High Dam]] in Egypt, including a plan to flood the valley containing the [[Abu Simbel]] temples, caused several conflicts.<ref>{{Cite web |date=21 July 2020 |title=Construction Of The Aswan High Dam In Egypt That Triggered The Suez Canal Conflict |url=https://voi.id/en/memori/9169 |access-date=2024-08-11 |website=VOI |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Muller |first=Mike |date=2020-07-30 |title=Plans for a dam across the Nile triggered a war in 1956: will it happen again? |url=http://theconversation.com/plans-for-a-dam-across-the-nile-triggered-a-war-in-1956-will-it-happen-again-143558 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200731003022/http://theconversation.com/plans-for-a-dam-across-the-nile-triggered-a-war-in-1956-will-it-happen-again-143558 |archive-date=July 31, 2020 |access-date=2024-08-11 |website=The Conversation |language=en-US}}</ref>

In 1959, after an appeal from the governments of [[Egypt]] and [[Sudan]], UNESCO launched an international safeguarding campaign. Archaeological research in the areas to be flooded was accelerated. And the Abu Simbel and [[Philae temple complex|Philae]] temples were dismantled, moved to dry ground, and reassembled.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Centre |first=UNESCO World Heritage |title=The World Heritage Convention |url=https://whc.unesco.org/en/convention/ |access-date=2024-08-11 |website=UNESCO World Heritage Centre |language=en}}</ref> The campaign cost about 80 million [[United States dollar|US dollars]], half of which was donated by some 50 countries.

Other safeguarding campaigns, such as saving [[Venetian Lagoon]] ([[Italy]]), the archaeological ruins at [[Mohenjo-daro]] (Pakistan), and restoring the [[Borobudur Temple Compounds]] ([[Indonesia]]), had been performed as well. Consequently, UNESCO initiated, with the help of the French cultural heritage organization, [[International Council on Monuments and Sites|ICOMOS]], the preparation of a draft convention on the protection of cultural heritage.

== Forms ==
Cultural heritage<ref>{{Cite web |title=Meaning of heritage in English |url=https://dictionary.cambridge.org/dictionary/english/heritage}}</ref> [[tourism]] involves visits to immovable historic sites which might include industrial sites such as [[fortification]]s, [[Transport|transportation facilities]], and other sites that might show the technologies of the past.<ref>Falser, Michael (2001). "Industrial Heritage Analysis" UNESCO World Heritage Center.</ref> The purchase of [[Cultural heritage|cultural goods]], including [[Royal Canadian Mint numismatic coins (1900–1999)|numismatic coins]], [[Bookselling|antiquarian books]], and [[antique]]s, can also be associated with heritage tourism when collectors travel to those locations.

Tourism organizations in these regions can offer specialized visits that allow tourists to experience the [[Gastronomy|gastronomic]] heritage associated with multiple brands.<ref>Aras, Sercan et al. (2015). [https://www.researchgate.net/publication/305396515_Gastronomy_in_Tourism "Gastronomy in Tourism"]. 3rd Global Conference on Business, Economics, Management, and Tourism. 26–28 November 2015, Rome, Italy.</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Gastronomy {{!}} UNWTO |url=https://www.unwto.org/gastronomy |access-date=2023-12-13 |website=www.unwto.org}}</ref> For example, [[Brittany]] ([[France]]), is associated with [[Galette]], while [[Normandy]] is associated with [[Calvados]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Are you a crêpe expert? |url=https://www.brittanytourism.com/matching-what-i-want/food-drink/brittanys-specialities/are-you-a-crepe-expert/ |access-date=2023-12-13 |website=Brittany tourism |language=en-GB}}</ref> In the [[United States]], the region known as the [[Bourbon County, Kentucky|Old Bourbon]] is associated with [[Bourbon whiskey]] production.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Bourbon – Kentucky Tourism – State of Kentucky – Visit Kentucky |url=https://www.kentuckytourism.com/things-to-do/bourbon |access-date=2023-12-13 |website=Kentucky Tourism |language=en}}</ref>
[[File:Archaeological dig at Ness of Brodgar (4855841735).jpg|thumb|An archaeologist from the [[UHI Archaeology Institute]] with heritage tourists at the [[Ness of Brodgar]]]]
[[Natural heritage]] tourism involves visits to natural features consisting of physical and biological formations or groups of such formations, [[Geological formation|geological]] and [[Physiographic region|physiographical]] formations and precisely delineated areas which constitute the [[habitat]] of [[Threatened species|threatened species of animals and plants]], natural sites, or precisely delineated natural areas.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Centre |first=UNESCO World Heritage |title=Convention Concerning the Protection of the World Cultural and Natural Heritage |url=https://whc.unesco.org/en/conventiontext/ |access-date=2024-08-11 |website=UNESCO World Heritage Centre |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Citation |last1=de la Calle Vaquero |first1=Manuel |title=Heritage Tourism and Visitor Management |date=2024-01-01 |encyclopedia=Encyclopedia of Archaeology (Second Edition) (Second Edition) |pages=597–605 |editor-last=Nikita |editor-first=Efthymia |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/B9780323907996000914 |access-date=2024-08-11 |place=Oxford |publisher=Academic Press |isbn=978-0-323-91856-5 |last2=García-Hernandez |first2=Maria |editor2-last=Rehren |editor2-first=Thilo}}</ref>

== Consequences ==
[[Benjamin W. Porter]] and [[Noel B. Salazar]] have [[ethnographically]] documented that cultural heritage tourism can create tensions and even conflict among the different stakeholders involved.<ref name="Porter and Salazar">
{{cite journal |author=Porter, Benjamin W. and Noel B. Salazar |year=2005 |title=Heritage tourism, conflict, and the public interest |url=https://lirias.kuleuven.be/handle/123456789/198861 |journal=International Journal of Heritage Studies |volume=11 |issue=5 |pages=361–370 |doi=10.1080/13527250500337397 |s2cid=145581442|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

The effect on [[indigenous peoples]] whose land and culture are being visited by tourists has been considered a problem. In Mexico, tourism increased because of the predicted [[2012 phenomenon|end of the Maya calendar]]. Some [[Activism|activists]]{{Who|date=August 2024}} claim the indigenous [[Maya peoples|Maya]] are not benefiting from the traffic.<ref>{{cite web |date=21 January 2012 |title=Mayans Demand Inclusion in 'Doomsday Tourism' |url=http://indiancountrytodaymedianetwork.com/2012/01/21/mayans-demand-inclusion-doomsday-tourism-73721 |access-date=4 April 2014 |work=[[Indian Country Today Media Network]]}}</ref> However, heritage tourism has sometimes contributed to the economies of certain regions, for example, heritage tourism contributed 50 million [[Pound sterling|pounds]] to [[Orkney]]'s economy in 2017.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Neolithic archaeology |url=https://www.uhi.ac.uk/en/research-enterprise/case-studies/neolithic-archaeology/ |access-date=2022-12-20 |website=University of the Highlands and Islands}}</ref>

Colonial officials employed fieldworkers' notes, books and fieldwork to understand aboriginal people.<ref>Restrepo, E., & Escobar, A. (2005). ‘Other Anthropologies and Anthropology Otherwise ’ Steps to a World Anthropologies Framework. ''[[Critique of Anthropology]]'', 25(2), 99–129.</ref><ref>Clifford, J., Dombrowski, K., Graburn, N., LeiteGoldberg, N., Phillips, R., Watkins, J., & Clifford, J. (2004). Looking several ways: Anthropology and native heritage in Alaska. ''[[Current Anthropology]]'', 45(1), 5–30.</ref>

=== UNESCO World Heritage Convention ===
Heritage tourism is promoted by the [[World Heritage Convention]], which is a part of [[UNESCO]]. This stemmed from various safeguarding campaigns. The decision to build the [[Aswan Dam|Aswan High Dam]] in Egypt, including a plan to flood the valley containing the [[Abu Simbel]] temples, caused several conflicts.<ref>{{Cite web |date=21 July 2020 |title=Construction Of The Aswan High Dam In Egypt That Triggered The Suez Canal Conflict |url=https://voi.id/en/memori/9169 |access-date=2024-08-11 |website=VOI |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Muller |first=Mike |date=2020-07-30 |title=Plans for a dam across the Nile triggered a war in 1956: will it happen again? |url=http://theconversation.com/plans-for-a-dam-across-the-nile-triggered-a-war-in-1956-will-it-happen-again-143558 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200731003022/http://theconversation.com/plans-for-a-dam-across-the-nile-triggered-a-war-in-1956-will-it-happen-again-143558 |archive-date=July 31, 2020 |access-date=2024-08-11 |website=The Conversation |language=en-US}}</ref>

In 1959, after an appeal from the governments of [[Egypt]] and [[Sudan]], UNESCO launched an international safeguarding campaign. Archaeological research in the areas to be flooded was accelerated. And the Abu Simbel and [[Philae temple complex|Philae]] temples were dismantled, moved to dry ground, and reassembled.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Centre |first=UNESCO World Heritage |title=The World Heritage Convention |url=https://whc.unesco.org/en/convention/ |access-date=2024-08-11 |website=UNESCO World Heritage Centre |language=en}}</ref> The campaign cost about 80 million [[United States dollar|US dollars]], half of which was donated by some 50 countries.

Other safeguarding campaigns, such as saving [[Venetian Lagoon]] ([[Italy]]), the archaeological ruins at [[Mohenjo-daro]] (Pakistan), and restoring the [[Borobudur Temple Compounds]] ([[Indonesia]]), had been performed as well. Consequently, UNESCO initiated, with the help of the French cultural heritage organization, [[International Council on Monuments and Sites|ICOMOS]], the preparation of a draft convention on the protection of cultural heritage.

W. |date=1978 |title=The Rediscovery of Herculaneum and Pompeii |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/41210458 |journal=The American Scholar |volume=47 |issue=4 |pages=461–470 |jstor=41210458 |issn=0003-0937}}</ref> Additionally, in the [[19th century]], there was an increase in tourism and in [[Grand Tour|grand tours of Europe]] to historical sites.<ref>{{Cite web |title=What was the Grand Tour? {{!}} Royal Museums Greenwich |url=https://www.rmg.co.uk/stories/topics/what-was-grand-tour |access-date=2023-12-13 |website=www.rmg.co.uk |language=en}}</ref> The concept of a [[Monument|historical monument]] emerged in the [[Western world]], accompanied by [[tourism]].<ref>{{Cite book |title=A Research Agenda for Heritage Tourism |publisher=Edward Elgar Publishing |year=2020 |isbn=9781789903522 |editor1=Maria Gravari-Barbas |pages=1}}</ref>

=== UNESCO World Heritage Convention ===
Heritage tourism is promoted by the [[World Heritage Convention]], which is a part of [[UNESCO]]. This stemmed from various safeguarding campaigns. === UNESCO World Heritage Convention ===
Heritage tourism is promoted by the [[World Heritage Convention]], which is a part of [[UNESCO]]. This stemmed from various safeguarding campaigns. The decision to build the [[Aswan Dam|Aswan High Dam]] in Egypt, including a plan to flood the valley containing the [[Abu Simbel]] temples, caused several conflicts.<ref>{{Cite web |date=21 July 2020 |title=Construction Of The Aswan High Dam In Egypt That Triggered The Suez Canal Conflict |url=https://voi.id/en/memori/9169 |access-date=2024-08-11 |website=VOI |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Muller |first=Mike |date=2020-07-30 |title=Plans for a dam across the Nile triggered a war in 1956: will it happen again? |url=http://theconversation.com/plans-for-a-dam-across-the-nile-triggered-a-war-in-1956-will-it-happen-again-143558 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200731003022/http://theconversation.com/plans-for-a-dam-across-the-nile-triggered-a-war-in-1956-will-it-happen-again-143558 |archive-date=July 31, 2020 |access-date=2024-08-11 |website=The Conversation |language=en-US}}</ref>

=== UNESCO World Heritage Convention ===
Heritage tourism is promoted by the [[World Heritage Convention]], which is a part of [[UNESCO]]. This stemmed from various safeguarding campaigns. The decision to build the [[Aswan Dam|Aswan High Dam]] in Egypt, including a plan to flood the valley containing the [[Abu Simbel]] temples, caused several conflicts.<ref>{{Cite web |date=21 July 2020 |title=Construction Of The Aswan High Dam In Egypt That Triggered The Suez Canal Conflict |url=https://voi.id/en/memori/9169 |access-date=2024-08-11 |website=VOI |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Muller |first=Mike |date=2020-07-30 |title=Plans for a dam across the Nile triggered a war in 1956: will it happen again? |url=http://theconversation.com/plans-for-a-dam-across-the-nile-triggered-a-war-in-1956-will-it-happen-again-143558 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200731003022/http://theconversation.com/plans-for-a-dam-across-the-nile-triggered-a-war-in-1956-will-it-happen-again-143558 |archive-date=July 31, 2020 |access-date=2024-08-11 |website=The Conversation |language=en-US}}</ref>

In 1959, after an appeal from the governments of [[Egypt]] and [[Sudan]], UNESCO launched an international safeguarding campaign. Archaeological research in the areas to be flooded was accelerated. And the Abu Simbel and [[Philae temple complex|Philae]] temples were dismantled, moved to dry ground, and reassembled.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Centre |first=UNESCO World Heritage |title=The World Heritage Convention |url=https://whc.unesco.org/en/convention/ |access-date=2024-08-11 |website=UNESCO World Heritage Centre |language=en}}</ref> The campaign cost about 80 million [[United States dollar|US dollars]], half of which was donated by some 50 countries.

Other safeguarding campaigns, such as saving [[Venetian Lagoon]] ([[Italy]]), the archaeological ruins at [[Mohenjo-daro]] (Pakistan), and restoring the [[Borobudur Temple Compounds]] ([[Indonesia]]), had been performed as well. Consequently, UNESCO initiated, with the help of the French cultural heritage organization, [[International Council on Monuments and Sites|ICOMOS]], the preparation of a draft convention on the protection of cultural heritage.

=== UNESCO World Heritage Convention ===
Heritage tourism is promoted by the [[World Heritage Convention]], which is a part of [[UNESCO]]. This stemmed from various safeguarding campaigns. The decision to build the [[Aswan Dam|Aswan High Dam]] in Egypt, including a plan to flood the valley containing the [[Abu Simbel]] temples, caused several conflicts.<ref>{{Cite web |date=21 July 2020 |title=Construction Of The Aswan High Dam In Egypt That Triggered The Suez Canal Conflict |url=https://voi.id/en/memori/9169 |access-date=2024-08-11 |website=VOI |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Muller |first=Mike |date=2020-07-30 |title=Plans for a dam across the Nile triggered a war in 1956: will it happen again? |url=http://theconversation.com/plans-for-a-dam-across-the-nile-triggered-a-war-in-1956-will-it-happen-again-143558 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200731003022/http://theconversation.com/plans-for-a-dam-across-the-nile-triggered-a-war-in-1956-will-it-happen-again-143558 |archive-date=July 31, 2020 |access-date=2024-08-11 |website=The Conversation |language=en-US}}</ref>

And the Abu Simbel and [[Philae temple complex|Philae]] temples were dismantled, moved to dry ground, and reassembled.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Centre |first=UNESCO World Heritage |title=The World Heritage Convention |url=https://whc.unesco.org/en/convention/ |access-date=2024-08-11 |website=UNESCO World Heritage Centre |language=en}}</ref> The campaign cost about 80 million [[United States dollar|US dollars]], half of which was donated by some 50 countries.  

Other safeguarding campaigns, such as saving [[Venetian Lagoon]] ([[Italy]]), the archaeological ruins at [[Mohenjo-daro]] (Pakistan), and restoring the [[Borobudur Temple Compounds]] ([[Indonesia]]), had been performed as well. Consequently, UNESCO initiated, with the help of the French cultural heritage organization, [[International Council on Monuments and Sites|ICOMOS]], the preparation of a draft convention on the protection of cultural heritage.

Some [[Activism|activists]]{{Who|date=August 2024}} claim the indigenous [[Maya peoples|Maya]] are not benefiting from the traffic.<ref>{{cite web |date=21 January 2012 |title=Mayans Demand Inclusion in 'Doomsday Tourism' |url=http://indiancountrytodaymedianetwork.com/2012/01/21/mayans-demand-inclusion-doomsday-tourism-73721 |access-date=4 April 2014 |work=[[Indian Country Today Media Network]]}}</ref> However, heritage tourism has sometimes contributed to the economies of certain regions, for example, heritage tourism contributed 50 million [[Pound sterling|pounds]] to [[Orkney]]'s economy in 2017.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Neolithic archaeology |url=https://www.uhi.ac.uk/en/research-enterprise/case-studies/neolithic-archaeology/ |access-date=2022-12-20 |website=University of the Highlands and Islands}}</ref>
